title: Idempotent Ensure Operation Rejecting an Already-Satisfied State
pattern: An additive or assigning operation whose purpose is to establish a state (create/ensure a directory, set a field to a value, acknowledge a message, mark as processed, enable or register something) returns an error or throws because that exact state already holds (`AlreadyExists`, `Unchanged`, `AlreadyAcked`, `AlreadySet`).
why_bad: The postcondition the caller asked for is already true, so the error carries no actionable information. Callers must pre-check (`if !path.exists()`, `if get() != v`), which adds boilerplate and a time-of-check/time-of-use race, or catch and discard the error. Under retries and at-least-once delivery, duplicate acks and repeated sets are routine, so the error breaks idempotent retry loops.
detection: A create, set, assign, ack, mark, enable or register function that compares the current state with the requested one (`path.exists()`, `current == new_value`, `set.contains(&id)`, `is_enabled`) and returns `Err`/throws when they already match, without an idempotent variant (`create_dir_all`, plain assignment, set insert). Removal, cleanup, stop and cancel operations on already-absent targets are a separate criterion and must not be flagged here.
counterexample: Operations where "already exists" is the signal the caller relies on: atomic exclusive creation used as a lock or claim (`create_new`, `mkdir` as mutex, `INSERT` guarded by a unique constraint), exactly-once transactional processors where a duplicate ack reveals a lost message elsewhere, and change-audit APIs that must reject no-op writes by specification.
source: John Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design*, Sections 10.2–10.3; Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Chapter 11; Marianne Bellotti, *Kill It with Fire*, Chapter 3.
